Argument quality is weak (39% of applicable dimensions held, no fallacies penalized), and the visibility and recruitment claims in Option A are unsupported assumptions, so the outcome should not rest on the debate winner's framing.", "conflict_severity": "medium", "stakeholder_analysis": [{"agent": "agent_1", "position": "Option A: 2000 € for an inter-city tournament with buffet and prizes, justified by expected visibility gains and new member recruitment (debate winner, but premise unsupported)", "influence": 0.4}, {"agent": "agent_2", "position": "Option B: 2000 € for pedagogical equipment (new chess sets, clocks, course materials), justified by the worn condition of current boards", "influence": 0.3}, {"agent": "agent_3", "position": "Option C: split 1000 € tournament and 1000 € equipment as a balanced compromise, though it does not show that each half reaches its goal", "influence": 0.3}], "recommended_resolution": "compromise", "governance_reasoning": "Social choice aggregation (for example a ranked or approval vote over A, B, C, and possibly a partial-funding variant) suits a discrete budget decision among competing options with three distinct stakeholders. The debate winner's Option A rests on untested assumptions about visibility and recruitment, so the vote should not defer to the debate result. Option C, the compromise, is the most likely to attract broad support, but the group should first test whether a reduced tournament still meets its aim and whether the equipment need really requires the full 2000 €. Gathering evidence such as recruitment history or replacement quotes would reduce the conflict before voting."}
